Focal–General Diffusion Model with Semantic Consistent Guidance for Sign
Language Production
Yiheng Yu1,2
Sheng Liu1,2*
Yuan Feng1,2
Zhelun Jin1,2
Yining Jiang1,2
Min Xu1,2
1Zhejiang University of Technology, Hangzhou, Zhejiang
2Zhejiang Key Laboratory of Visual Information Intelligent Processing
{yhyu, edliu, fengyuan, zljin, ynjiang, mxu2019}@zjut.edu.cn
Abstract
Sign Language Production (SLP) aims to translate spoken
language into sign sequences, where the main challenge
lies in generating coherent and natural poses from dis-
crete glosses (G2P). Existing G2P methods typically treat
each pose as an indivisible unit, limiting their ability to
capture fine-grained joint-level dependencies and thus de-
grading pose quality. To address this, we propose the Fo-
cal–General Diffusion Model (FGDM), characterized by
a pioneering two-stage denoising framework that harmo-
nizes local joint-level dependencies and global coherence.
Specifically, in the Focal stage, a novel Adaptive Sign GCN
(ASGCN) adaptively models each pose based on contextual
correlations, skeletal topology, and semantic conditions,
ensuring precise generation of local details. In the Gen-
eral stage, a Transformer-based module refines the entire
pose sequence to enhance global coherence and natural-
ness. Moreover, we introduce a Semantic Consistent Guid-
ance (SCG) mechanism that seamlessly integrates semantic
supervision into diffusion training, enforcing tighter align-
ment between generated pose sequences and their intended
gloss semantics. Extensive experiments on PHOENIX14T
and USTC-CSL demonstrate that FGDM achieves SOTA
performance. Our project page is available at here.
1. Introduction
Sign Language Production (SLP) plays a crucial role in pro-
moting communication, education, and the broader adop-
tion of sign languages [2, 3, 46].
However, due to the
unique grammatical structures of sign languages and the
complex, fine-grained movements they involve, existing
methods struggle to generate accurate and realistic sign se-
quences directly. To address this challenge, previous studies
[20, 31, 39, 41] typically decompose the task into two stages
for pose generation (shown in Fig. 1 Top): Text-to-Gloss

Figure 1. Top: Illustration pipeline of SLP, including T2G and
G2P. T2G converts text into glosses, while G2P maps each gloss
to its corresponding pose sequence and generates smooth transi-
tions to ensure naturalness. This work primarily focuses on G2P.
Bottom: Comparison with existing methods on the challenging
PHOENIX14T [5] dataset. Our approach achieves new SOTA re-
sults across all metrics on both DEV and TEST sets.
(T2G) and Gloss-to-Pose (G2P). The former has been ef-
fectively tackled using NMT-based methods [24, 25], while
the latter remains considerably more challenging and thus
carries greater research significance. Furthermore, the gen-
erated pose sequences from the G2P stage can be used to
animate digital avatars or serve as the foundation for sign
video synthesis. Motivated by these factors, this work fo-
cuses on advancing the G2P task.
Recently, increasing efforts have been devoted to im-
proving G2P methods.
Saunders et al.
[31] introduced
the first end-to-end approach, a Progressive Transformer for
This CVPR paper is the Open Access version, provided by the Computer Vision Foundation.
Except for this watermark, it is identical to the accepted version;
the final published version of the proceedings is available on IEEE Xplore.
35915

G2P, and later enhanced it with adversarial training to pro-
duce more realistic results [32, 33]. However, the autore-
gressive design of Saunders’ model leads to error accumu-
lation. To address this issue, Hwang et al. [21] proposed a
non-autoregressive Transformer that maps gloss sequences
directly to pose sequences, while Huang et al. [20] fur-
ther introduced an External Aligner to improve sequence
alignment learning in non-autoregressive models. More re-
cently, diffusion-based methods have emerged: Xie et al.
[47] proposed a discrete diffusion model for G2P, Tang et al.
[42] enhanced diffusion generation stability through multi-
hypothesis aggregation, and in their subsequent work [41],
incorporated feature disentanglement into the diffusion pro-
cess to better capture decoupled attributes. However, exist-
ing SOTA methods [39–42, 47] overemphasize global mod-
eling and fail to capture fine-grained joint-level dependen-
cies, leading to degraded pose quality.
Additionally, ensuring the semantic consistency of gen-
erated pose sequences is crucial, as it directly determines
the intelligibility and expressiveness of sign language gen-
eration. However, advanced diffusion architectures [15, 40–
42, 47] can only blindly fit coordinates under regression-
based supervision, failing to guarantee semantic consis-
tency.
Although a few early studies have investigated
semantic-guided generation in non-diffusion models [20,
39], these approaches suffer from large cross-modal align-
ment gaps, which severely affect training stability and over-
all performance. Moreover, due to the unique character-
istics of diffusion training, previous methods cannot be
directly transferred to diffusion-based models.
In gen-
eral, how to effectively leverage semantic signals for cross-
modal guidance, particularly within diffusion frameworks,
remains an open question.
To address the aforementioned challenges, we propose a
Focal–General Diffusion Model (FGDM) with a Seman-
tic Consistent Guidance (SCG) mechanism for the G2P
task in SLP. 1) To enhance the model’s awareness of fine-
grained dependencies, FGDM originally adopts a two-stage
denoising paradigm: a Focal stage that models joint-level
dependencies, and a General stage that enables global se-
quence coherence. In the Focal stage, we reformulate the
graph convolution and introduce the Adaptive Sign GCN
(ASGCN), which innovatively incorporates contextual cor-
relations and semantic conditions for adaptive pose model-
ing. In the General stage, skeletal representations are pro-
jected into a higher-level space, allowing the Transformer-
based module to enhance global naturalness and coherence.
2) To bridge the gap in cross-modal semantic supervision,
SCG introduces a new perspective: it jointly trains a seman-
tic decoder that maps the generated pose features into the
semantic space. In this space, pose features are effectively
aligned with gloss sequences by maximizing the likelihood
over all feasible alignment paths, following the principle of
Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) [12]. More-
over, to adapt to diffusion training, SCG dynamically ad-
justs the supervision strength according to the current sam-
pling stage, ensuring stable model convergence. As shown
in Fig. 1, FGDM trained with SCG achieves SOTA results
across all metrics on the challenging PHOENIX14T bench-
mark, confirming the effectiveness of our method.
2. Related Work
2.1. Sign Language Production
Sign language production (SLP), as the inverse of recogni-
tion [14, 18, 19, 29, 51] and translation [7, 8, 53], directly
benefits the Deaf community and also supports the promo-
tion and teaching of sign language. With the increasing de-
mand, research interest in SLP has been steadily growing
[30, 45].
Early approaches to SLP relied on avatar-based tech-
nologies [11, 23] and Statistical Machine Translation
(SMT) [24, 25], but these methods were costly and in-
flexible.
Stoll et al.
[38] first introduced deep learn-
ing and decomposing SLP into three subproblems: Text-
to-Gloss (T2G), Gloss-to-Pose (G2P), and Pose-to-Video
(P2V), with G2P receiving the most attention due to its
cross-modal challenges and practical value.
Saunders et
al. [31] proposed the first end-to-end G2P model, Progress
Transformer, and later enhanced it with GANs and Mixture
Density Networks [32, 34]. Subsequent research [20, 21]
has underscored the inherent limitations of autoregressive
models (e.g., error accumulation, regression to the mean),
thereby motivating the exploration of non-regressive alter-
natives. Recently, diffusion models have been applied to
G2P. Xie et al.
[47] employed discrete denoising diffu-
sion for discretized pose representations, while Tang et al.
[41] introduced an iconicity-disentangled diffusion frame-
work that maps 3D joints into 4D bones. However, cur-
rent methods typically ignore joint-level dependencies and
solely rely on regression losses, which severely degrade
generation quality. To overcome these limitations, we in-
troduce FGDM with an SCG supervision mechanism.
2.2. Graph Convolutional Networks
Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) [4] can effectively
capture both topological structures and node attributes in
graph data, making them well-suited for skeleton-based
tasks. In Skeleton-Based Action Recognition, Yan et al.
[48] introduced ST-GCN, the first framework to leverage
graph convolution for modeling spatiotemporal skeleton dy-
namics. This pioneering work inspired a series of follow-
up studies [9, 10, 26, 36, 37].
Among them, Shi et al.
[36] introduced the Adaptive Graph Convolutional Net-
work (AGCN), where the adjacency matrix is dynamically
learned rather than predefined. It was later extended with a
multi-stream architecture and refined attention mechanisms

Figure 2. Overall pipeline of FGDM during training and inference. In training, the noisy sequence Xt is generated by adding noise to the
target sequence X0 for t steps. FGDM denoises Xt under glosses guidance to predict the initial sequence ˆ
X0. It comprises two stages:
a Focal stage for joint-level dependency modeling and a General stage for global sequence modeling. Beyond the standard regression
loss, Semantic Consistent Guidance (SCG) provides auxiliary supervision, where the V2S Adapter and Semantic Decoder project visual
features into the semantic space, and the SCG loss enforces tighter consistency with the gloss sequence. During inference, FGDM iteratively
denoises random inputs to generate sign sequences.
to further boost performance [37]. In sign language recog-
nition (SLR), ST-GCN has been widely adopted. Jiao et
al.
[22] leveraged multiple ST-GCNs to capture region-
specific body dynamics, whereas Li et al. [27] adopted ST-
GCN as a robust pose encoder. For SLP, Saunders et al.
[35] developed a graph-based pose decoder, Huang et al.
[20] integrated ST-GCN as the generator head, and He et
al. [15] proposed a diffusion-based architecture built upon
ST-GCN. However, the frame-shared GCN paradigm is sub-
optimal for SLP, as joint semantics and spatial dependency
strength dynamically change over time, making static meth-
ods incapable of adapting flexibly. To address this, we pro-
pose a novel frame-wise adaptive GCN, ASGCN, to achieve
flexible and precise sign pose modeling in the Focal stage.
3. Methodology
3.1. Overview
Given a gloss sequence G = {gi}L
i=1 containing L glosses,
our objective is to generate the corresponding sign pose se-
quence X = {xi}S
i=1 with S frames, where each xi ∈
RJ×3 represents the 3D coordinates of J keypoints. As
illustrated in Fig. 2, the proposed Focal–General Diffu-
sion Model (FGDM) presents the overall architecture as
well as the training and inference pipelines. The key in-
novation of this framework lies in constructing a novel de-
noising network, enabling progressive modeling from local
joint dependencies to global sequence coherence. More-
over, the Semantic Consistent Guidance (SCG) ensures
consistency between the generated sequence and the seman-
tic conditions. The following describes each component.
3.2. Focal–General Diffusion Model
As a diffusion-based model, FGDM comprises two Markov
chains during training: a diffusion process and a denoising
process. In the diffusion process, the 3D target pose se-
quence X0 ∈RS×J×3 is gradually corrupted by Gaussian
noise ϵ ∼N(0, I) for t steps, resulting in a noisy sequence
Xt. Following DDPMs [16], this process is formulated as:
Q(Xt|X0) := √¯atX0 + ϵ
√
1 −¯at,
t ∼U(0, T),
(1)
where T denotes the maximum diffusion sample steps,
¯at := Qt
s=0 as, and as := 1 −βs. Here, βs represents
the cosine noise variance schedule. During inference, Xt is
directly sampled from a Gaussian distribution. As the main
innovation lies in the denoising process, we focus on intro-
ducing this part as follows.
Embedding.
We first apply Iconicity Disentangle-
ment [41] to Xt ∈RS×J×3 to obtain an enhanced rep-
resentation X′
t ∈RS×J×7. Then, X′
t is embedded into
Xe
t ∈RS×J×d through an embedding matrix. Meanwhile,
the gloss sequence is processed by the Gloss Encoder [42],
whose output is fused with the time embedding to generate
the gloss feature G ∈RL×c.
Focal Stage. As illustrated in Fig. 2, the Focal stage pri-
marily comprises L1 stacked layers of ASGCN and TCN.
ASGCN primarily models spatial joint dependencies, while
TCN focuses on temporal joint dynamics, following the
space–time decomposition design [36, 48]. Since ASGCN
is our core contribution, we detail it below.
ASGCN. Conventional static graph convolutions [26,
36, 37, 48] are insufficient to model the dynamic variations
in joint semantics and spatial dependencies inherent in sign

According to the above formulation, since the adjacency

Ai = (Ai

(3)

We next describe these three components in detail.
(a) Get Ai
a. Modeling multi-frame contextual correla-
tions enables the GCN to infer dynamic, context-aware joint
dependencies, resulting in more coherent and accurate rep-
resentations for the current frame. As shown in Fig. 3 (a),
for the i-th frame Xi, we compute its correlations with itself
and its n neighboring frames as follows:
Ci = { WψXi · WτXi+j | j ∈[−n, n] },
(4)
where Ci ∈R(2n+1)×J×J, and Wψ and Wτ denote two
distinct convolution for embedding. We then aggregate the
(2n + 1) correlation matrices in Ci to obtain Ai
a:
Ai
a = σ(Ci) · WAgg,
(5)
where the sigmoid function σ(·) serve as a gating
mechanism and ensures numerical stability.
WAgg
∈
R(2n+1)×Kv denotes a linear layer that adaptively weights
and integrates correlations. Note that WAgg is initialized to
zero, allowing the model to gradually incorporate Ai
a.
(b) Get Ai
b. The purpose of Ai
b is to preserve the skeletal
prior topology and enhance structural stability. As shown
in Fig. 3 (b), we first set the neck joint as the root to estab-
lish the skeletal hierarchy. We then apply Spatial Separa-
tion [48] to decompose the topology into Kv submatrices,
which are subsequently normalized to initialize Ai
b. As Ai
b
encodes the physical topology, it remains consistent and is
shared across all frames.
(c) Get Mi. Since sign poses with different semantics
may exhibit distinct joint dependency strengths, we con-
struct a semantic mask Mi to align the graph structure with
the corresponding semantics. As shown in Fig. 3 (c), for
a gloss feature sequence G = G1, G2, . . . , GL, we build
a corresponding mask set M = M 1, M 2, . . . , M L, which
serves as prototype masks for generating Mi:
M = {MG(Gl) | l ∈[1, L]},
(6)
the mask generator MG(·) maps each gloss feature into a
J × J mask, and this mapping is currently realized through

General Stage. The General stage models long-range

3.3. Semantic Consistent Guidance
SCG uniquely introduces semantic guidance into diffusion
training, bridging the cross-modal gap and ensuring strong
semantic consistency in the generated pose sequences.
As shown in Fig. 2, for the visual features XGo
t
output
from the General stage, the V2S Adapter first performs an
intermediate visual-to-semantic transition:
Xtrans
t
= V 2S Adapter(Xgo
t ),
(15)
where V 2S Adapter(·) consists of two linear layers and a
ReLU activation. Xtrans
t
∈RS×dg is then decoded into the
semantic space by the Semantic Decoder.
The architecture of the Semantic Decoder is inspired by
advances in sign language recognition [19, 28, 49, 50]. As
illustrated in Fig. 2, it consists of three main components:
a Local Semantic Decoder (LSD), a Global Semantic De-
coder (GSD), and a Gloss Classifier, defined as follows:

model local features, producing yl

S/2. GSD(·) employs a BiLSTM to capture global depen-
dencies, and the final outputs is yo

where num glosses + 1 denotes all glosses plus an addi-
tional blank label for alignment.

4. Experiments
4.1. Experimental Setup
4.1.1. Datasets
PHOENIX14T [5] is the most widely used dataset for SLP.
It comprises 2,887 unique German words and 1,066 distinct
signs, totaling 8,257 German weather forecast samples with
corresponding annotations. The dataset is partitioned into
7,096 training, 519 validation, and 642 testing samples.
USTC-CSL [13] is a Chinese sign language dataset that
has been adopted in recent SLP studies [15, 40, 41].
It
contains 100 unique sentences performed by 50 signers and
provides two official data splits: Split-I (4,000 training and
1,000 testing samples) and Split-II (4,700 training and 300
testing samples). Previous SLP methods [15, 40, 41] used
only Split-I, where test sentences overlap with the training
set. In this work, we evaluate on both Split-I and the more
challenging Split-II.
4.1.2. Evaluation Metrics.
Following previous works [20, 39, 42, 47], the generated
sign poses are back-translated into gloss sequences and text
using a sign language translation model [5]. The outputs are
then evaluated against the references using WER, BLEU,
and ROUGE. Moreover, FID is also employed to assess the
quality of the generated results. These evaluation metrics
are described in more detail in the supplementary materials.
4.1.3. Implementation Details.
Following prior works [20, 39, 42, 47], we first use Open-
Pose [6] to extract 50 human 2D keypoints per frame from
PHOENIX14T. The keypoints are then converted into 3D
coordinates using a skeletal correction model [52] to serve
as the ground truth. For USTC-CSL, which provides 25 hu-
man 3D keypoints per frame, normalization is applied, and
the processed data are used as the ground truth. For model
evaluation, we adopt NSLT [5], which translates the gen-
erated pose sequences into gloss sequences and spoken lan-
guage. To ensure fair comparison, we use the NSLT weights
from [41] on PHOENIX14T. Since pretrained weights for
USTC-CSL are unavailable, we retrain the model and re-
produce all compared methods for consistent and fair eval-
uation. In addition, the diffusion model is trained with 1000

use the Adam optimizer [1] with a learning rate of 0.001.
The n in Eq. 4 is set to 3, α in Eq. 17 is set to 10, while λ
and γ in Eq. 19 are set to 0.1 and 0.0001, respectively. All
experiments are conducted on 1 NVIDIA A6000 GPU.
4.2. Comparison with State-of-the-Arts
We evaluate FGDM on two datasets, PHOENIX14T and
USTC-CSL.
PHOENIX14T. Tab. 1 presents the comparison between
FGDM and existing SLP methods on the PHOENIX14T.
According to whether diffusion models are used, meth-
ods are grouped into Non-Diffusion Based and Diffusion
Based. FGDM consistently outperforms all baselines across
all metrics, achieving new SOTA results.
Specifically,
compared with the strongest non-diffusion method GEN-
OBT, FGDM shows notable gains of +2.0%/+3.43% (DE-
V/TEST) on BLEU-1, +3.66%/+4.96% on ROUGE, and
-10.14%/-11.08% on WER. Even among diffusion-based
models, FGDM remains dominant, surpassing the best-
performing Sign-IDD by +2.36%/+3.94% in ROUGE and
reducing WER by -6.86%/-8.45%.
Interestingly, FGDM
achieves a lower WER than Ground Truth, likely because
1) its generated poses are closer to the training distribution,
aiding recognition, and 2) it can correct mislabeled ground
truth samples (see Fig. 4 (c)). These comparison results
highlight the strong performance of FGDM.
USTC-CSL. Since most existing methods only report re-
sults on PHOENIX14T, we compare FGDM with available
open-source methods on USTC-CSL. As shown in the Tab.
2, FGDM consistently outperforms others on both Split-I
and Split-II. Specifically, on Split-I, although FGDM and
Sign-IDD achieve the same FID of 0.07, FGDM surpasses
Sign-IDD on all other metrics, with BLEU-1 and BLEU-4
improved by +1.51% and +3.92%, respectively, and WER

4.3. Ablation Study
We perform ablations on the PHOENIX14T to evaluate the
proposed methods.
Ablations for the main innovations.
As shown in
Tab. 3, we take the General stage as the baseline and pro-
gressively incorporate the other components.
According
to the results, both components consistently enhance per-
formance. Introducing the Focal stage boosts BLEU-1 to
28.09% and BLEU-4 to 9.84% on the DEV, while reducing
WER by -4.43%/-5.85% (DEV/TEST). Adding the SCG
strategy also significantly improves all metrics. When Focal
and SCG are combined, the model achieves the best results,
with WER reductions of -8.78%/-9.06% compared to the
baseline. Overall, both Focal and SCG contribute to higher-
quality pose generation, and their combination yields the
best results.
Ablations for parameters L1 and L2. We investigate
the impact of the stacked layer numbers in the Focal and
General stages. As shown in Tab. 4, increasing L1 consis-
tently improves performance, with L1 = 3 achieving the
best BLEU-1, BLEU-4, and WER on DEV and optimal
BLEU-4 on TEST. Further increases bring negligible gains
(+0.02% BLEU-1, –0.28% WER). For L2, the best results
are obtained when L2 = 2. Therefore, we adopt L1 = 3
and L2 = 2 as the final configuration.
Ablations for Ai
a, Ai
b, and Mi in Eq. 3. As shown
in Tab. 5, we ablate the core components of Eq. 3 in AS-
GCN. Ai
a, Ai
b, and Mi are generated based on contextual
correlations, skeletal topology, and semantic conditions, re-
spectively. Removing any of them degrades performance.
Excluding Ai
a causes the largest drop (BLEU-1: -4.80%/-
4.16%; WER: +2.59%/+4.56%), followed by Mi (BLEU-
1: -3.09%/-2.83%; WER: +1.09%/+3.29%). Above results
demonstrate the effectiveness of combining Ai
a, Ai
b, and
Mi, with the correlation term Ai
a and semantic mask Mi
being most critical to ASGCN’s performance.

4.4. Qualitative Results
Qualitative comparison with previous methods.
As
shown in Fig. 4, we compare the generated results of FGDM
with PT-GN and Sign-IDD on the PHOENIX14T. Since PT-
GN and Sign-IDD neglect fine-grained dependencies, their
generated poses are less accurate and natural, especially
in the zoomed-in regions (a) and (b), where densely con-
nected hand joints are difficult to model precisely. In con-
trast, FGDM dynamically captures joint-level dependencies
through the Focal stage, producing more natural and GT-
consistent hand shapes and overall poses. Notably, in panels
(b) and (c), even when the GT is corrupted by occlusion or
motion blur, FGDM still produces results that are closer to
the raw image. This robustness partly arise from our SCG
strategy, which semantically mitigates the impact of inac-
curate GT during training. Overall, FGDM demonstrates
superior realism and robustness with previous methods.
Qualitative comparison between w/o and w/ Focal. As
shown in Fig. 5, without the Focal stage, the model strug-
gles to capture joint-level dependencies, resulting in un-
natural and distorted hand shapes due to the complex cor-
relations among hand joints. In contrast, with the Focal
stage, the model learns intricate joint relationships through
the ASGCN and generates more natural and accurate ges-
tures—for example, correctly producing the extended index
finger in the first case and the clenched fist in the second.
These results demonstrate that the Focal stage effectively
models joint-level dependencies and enhances fine-grained
pose accuracy.
5. Conclusions
This paper presents a novel Focal–General Diffusion Model
(FGDM) with a Semantic Consistent Guidance (SCG)
mechanism for Sign Language Production (SLP). Specifi-
cally, FGDM introduces a pioneering two-stage denoising
framework that effectively balances joint-level dependen-
cies and global coherence.
In the Focal stage, we pro-
pose the Adaptive Sign GCN (ASGCN), which reformu-
lates graph convolution to enable frame-wise adaptive pose
modeling. Furthermore, SCG seamlessly integrates seman-
tic supervision into diffusion training, enforcing tighter se-
mantic consistency between generated poses and gloss se-
quences. Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments
demonstrate that FGDM surpasses existing SOTA methods
by a clear margin. We hope this work can inspire future
research to further explore the potential of diffusion frame-
works in SLP from new perspectives.
